clinicalPearls: Caused by mutations in CD40LG on the X chromosome encoding CD40 ligand (CD154), expressed on activated T cells, so the disorder is X-linked and affects males.
Failure of CD40 ligand to engage CD40 on B cells abolishes immunoglobulin class-switch recombination and germinal-centre formation, producing low or absent IgG, IgA and IgE with normal or raised IgM.

Because the same CD40-CD40 ligand interaction licenses macrophages and dendritic cells, it behaves as a combined immunodeficiency with susceptibility to opportunistic pathogens, not merely an antibody deficiency.
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a common presenting infection in infancy and warrants prophylaxis from diagnosis.
Cryptosporidium infection is characteristic and drives sclerosing cholangitis and a markedly increased risk of biliary tract and liver malignancy.
Chronic or cyclical neutropenia is frequent and can cause oral ulceration and worsen infection risk.

Management combines immunoglobulin replacement, Pneumocystis prophylaxis, scrupulous avoidance of Cryptosporidium (including boiled or filtered water), and consideration of haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which can be curative.
Serum IgM may be normal rather than elevated, so the pattern of low switched isotypes with preserved or high IgM, not the IgM level alone, defines the syndrome.
reference.pathophysiology: CD40 ligand (CD154) is a tumour necrosis factor family molecule transiently expressed on the surface of activated CD4 T cells. Its engagement of CD40 on B cells within germinal centres delivers the co-stimulatory signal required for immunoglobulin class-switch recombination and somatic hypermutation, enabling B cells to switch from IgM production to high-affinity IgG, IgA and IgE. Loss-of-function mutations in CD40LG abolish this signal, so B cells remain locked in IgM production and germinal centres fail to form, giving low switched immunoglobulins with normal or raised IgM. Crucially, CD40-CD40 ligand signalling also activates monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells and supports effective T-cell priming; its absence impairs cell-mediated defence against intracellular and opportunistic organisms such as Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptosporidium species and mycobacteria. The same pathway influences myelopoiesis, contributing to the neutropenia frequently observed. The combined humoral and cellular defect, together with chronic Cryptosporidium-driven biliary injury, accounts for the infective, hepatobiliary and malignant complications that distinguish this condition from purely antibody-deficient hyper-IgM syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: CD40 deficiency (autosomal recessive hyper-IgM with an identical functional phenotype)
Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AICDA) deficiency (intrinsic B-cell class-switch defect, no opportunistic infection)
NEMO (IKBKG) deficiency with hyper-IgM and ectodermal dysplasia
Common variable immunodeficiency with raised IgM
Other combined immunodeficiencies presenting with Pneumocystis pneumonia
Secondary hyper-IgM states such as congenital infection
additionalInvestigations: Serum immunoglobulin profile showing low IgG and IgA with normal or raised IgM
Flow cytometry for CD40 ligand expression on activated CD4 T cells (reduced or absent, using a functional stimulation assay)
CD40LG gene sequencing to confirm the mutation and enable carrier testing
Full blood count to detect associated neutropenia
Stool and molecular testing for Cryptosporidium and liver function tests with biliary imaging where cholangitis is suspected
Specific antibody responses to protein and polysaccharide vaccines demonstrating impaired switched responses
HLA typing of patient and family when transplantation is considered
redFlags: Pneumocystis pneumonia or other opportunistic infection in an infant or young boy
Persistent diarrhoea with Cryptosporidium and deranged liver function suggesting sclerosing cholangitis
Neutropenia with oral ulceration or perianal sepsis
Progressive hepatobiliary disease or features suggesting biliary or hepatic malignancy
Recurrent sinopulmonary infection with the hyper-IgM immunoglobulin pattern
reference.prognosis: With immunoglobulin replacement, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and Cryptosporidium avoidance many patients reach adulthood, but progressive sclerosing cholangitis, liver disease and biliary or hepatic malignancy remain major causes of morbidity and death. Early haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be curative and is most successful before significant organ damage develops.
pitfalls: Labelling the disorder a pure antibody deficiency underestimates the risk of Pneumocystis and other opportunistic infections and delays prophylaxis.
Serum IgM is not always elevated, so a normal IgM does not exclude the diagnosis when switched isotypes are low.
Overlooking Cryptosporidium exposure allows preventable sclerosing cholangitis and malignancy risk to accrue.
Associated neutropenia may be misattributed to infection rather than the underlying disorder.
Failure to consider CD40 deficiency means autosomal recessive girls with the same phenotype can be missed.
